title: Evidence Is the Antidote in Education
author: Holly Korbey
summary: Korbey argues that American parents and schools rely on vague, visible clues about school quality — buildings, extracurriculars, 'vibes' — because actual learning is invisible and hard to measure, and that this fantasy-based decision-making is finally starting to give way to an evidence-based approach borrowed from medicine. Drawing on Helen Pearson's book Beyond Belief, she traces how the 'evidence revolution' that transformed medicine through the Cochrane Collaboration's systematic reviews arrived in education roughly two decades ago, with England's Education Endowment Foundation running over 160 randomized controlled trials and building a widely used Teaching and Learning Toolkit. The piece contrasts England's success embedding evidence into teacher training and school leadership with the US's comparatively ignored What Works Clearinghouse, once nicknamed the 'Nothing Works Clearinghouse' because so few popular classroom interventions held up under testing. Korbey closes by calling for the same evidence base to be marketed to the American public the way public health facts are — loudly and repeatedly — so parents and teachers stop relying on fantasy and start relying on what's actually been shown to work.
points: England's 85% head-teacher usage rate for the EEF's Teaching and Learning Toolkit versus the US's largely untracked, ignored use of the What Works Clearinghouse is presented as the key structural difference explaining why evidence-based teaching took hold in one country and not the other.

The claim that 'a lot of education is done on vibes' (via Carl Hendrick) reframes seemingly positive signals — happy kids, good energy — as unreliable proxies that tell parents nothing about whether actual learning is happening.

The argument draws a direct structural parallel between pre-evidence-revolution medicine (opinion-based treatment decisions) and pre-evidence-revolution education, suggesting education is roughly one generation behind medicine in adopting systematic review methodology.

The piece's closing prescription — treat evidence-based teaching facts (retrieval practice works, learning styles don't, teacher effectiveness is the single biggest in-school factor) as public-health-style information campaigns — is a concrete policy move, not just a research call.
quotes: But learning itself is often invisible, and happens inside each individual student's head. So parents are left with fantasies and clues.
A lot of education is done on vibes. In other words, I feel like I'm doing a really good thing. The kids are feeling like they're having a good time, so what's the problem?

Before that, groundbreaking doctor Iain Chalmers told Pearson, decisions about treatment were often based on "someone's opinion or conventional wisdom." He was convinced that he had harmed patients by giving treatment advice that could have been wrong.

When the Institute of Educational Sciences (IES) and its research homebase, the What Works Clearinghouse, first launched in the early 2000s to provide reviews of evidence for teaching and learning practices, Pearson notes, it was dubbed the "Nothing Works Clearinghouse" because when actually tested, so few of the popular interventions used in American schools were shown to have any evidence of efficacy behind them.
According to the EEF, 85% of English head teachers (principals) refer to the toolkit when making decisions about teaching and learning for their students.
We have the antidote to fantasies in education. Now we just need to use it.
